The word Arab here does not mean belonging through pure blood or descent. That kind of pure descent has ceased to have any meaningful place in history.

Instead, the word refers to the historical features associated with the forms of civilization produced by the Arab historical movement and by the interaction between the Arabs and the many peoples who took part with them in creating those forms and their history.
The word Islamic, in turn, points precisely to this wider participation and to those peoples themselves.
Its meaning here is therefore civilizational, not religious.

This shared history was created by a complex and interconnected social structure. Its political, legal, and legislative order was tied to the system of the Islamic Caliphate and to the material and economic foundations on which that system rested.
This did not mean that everyone living within the society of the Caliphate was necessarily Muslim by belief.
History tells us that many followed other religions and systems of belief: Christianity, Judaism, Sabianism, Mazdakism, and others.
So when we use the word Islamic here, we are referring only to a social and historical meaning.
If the best description we have for this shared history is Arab-Islamic, in the sense just explained, then its intellectual heritage in all its different forms must also be Arab-Islamic.
According to the analysis we have just given, even the language of that heritage is Arab-Islamic in this historical sense.
Here, then, the philosophy of the heritage reveals its real historical identity.
It is not Islamic in a purely religious sense.
Nor is it purely Islamic in a historical sense.
It is Arab-Islamic philosophy, in the meaning we have developed above.
That is the meaning of the term we have adopted throughout this book.
A — The Pre-Islamic Period Between Two Stages

We begin our study with the pre-Islamic period, or Jāhiliyya, because we want to trace the earliest historical roots of the ways people in the Arabian Peninsula understood the universe and nature, as well as their social relationships and conditions of life. These were the first forms of what we might call Arab thought or Arab culture before Islam.

Starting here will help us follow the history of this thought from its beginnings. Later, this will give us a basis for understanding the larger course of its development after Islam, through the many breaks, leaps, and transformations that took place in Arab history.

But there is another, less direct reason for beginning with the pre-Islamic period. In fact, this second starting point is essential if we want to understand its intellectual and cultural life. We must look at the structure of tribal society in the Arabian Peninsula, the material foundations on which that structure rested, and the forms it took during this period.
Here, however, our discussion is limited to the particular historical stage with which this chapter begins: the final stage of the pre-Islamic period.

Arab history before Islam can be divided into two main stages. Historians and researchers broadly agree that the later stage—the one that concerns us here—does not extend much further back than the fifth and sixth centuries CE. Historical works, whether written by Orientalists or others, generally discuss the period directly preceding the rise of Islam within these two centuries.
There are solid reasons for drawing the line here. Two facts in particular help explain it.

The first is pre-Islamic poetry, which is still regarded as our most reliable source for studying this period. Historians of Arabic literature have found no surviving poetry that can confidently be dated to more than about 150 years before Islam.

This is an important historical fact. The images, attitudes, relationships, descriptions, and views of the world found in this poetry correspond closely to what we know about Arab tribal life in the final part of the pre-Islamic period. We do not find in it reflections of the much older forms of life revealed by archaeology or by classical Greek and Roman historians, especially those that existed before the fifth century CE.
At the same time, the highly developed form of the pre-Islamic poetry that has reached us clearly suggests a much longer history behind it. It could not have appeared suddenly in the form we know.

But the fact that no earlier poetry has survived also suggests that the poetry available to us belongs historically to the same period of pre-Islamic Arab history that later Muslim writers were especially concerned with. So it is reasonable to use the age of this poetry as a rough measure for the period we are studying.

The second fact comes from comparing the economic and social conditions of the Arabian Peninsula in the fifth and sixth centuries with those of earlier periods. Modern historical discoveries show a clear difference between the two stages.
We can describe that difference as follows:

In the fifth and sixth centuries, the societies of the Arabian Peninsula were mainly organized through tribal bonds. The population was divided into separate tribal groups, usually connected by descent and sometimes by alliances. These tribes remained independent of one another. There were no political institutions uniting them, and no tribe accepted an authority from outside itself.

For most tribes, camel herding was a main source of livelihood and production. Some also depended on agriculture where natural conditions made it possible, as in Yemen, Hadramawt, the coasts of Oman, some towns of the Hijaz such as Taif and Yathrib and their surrounding areas, as well as Yamama and the oases.

Nomadic life therefore remained more common than settled life based on agriculture. Later, we will see new forces begin to change this picture and partially weaken the old tribal system. But those changes did not alter the basic character of the historical stage as a whole.

Before the fifth and sixth centuries, the evidence available to modern researchers, archaeologists, and historians leaves little room for doubt that parts of the Arabian Peninsula—especially the south—had reached relatively advanced levels of agriculture, artificial irrigation, architecture, political organization in the form of states, and division of labor. The population included farmers, livestock herders, and craftsmen.
Some traces of these conditions survived into the fifth century, though by then they were already in decline.

Engels appears to have come across some of this evidence as early as the middle of the nineteenth century. In a letter to Marx dated 24 May 1853, he wrote: “It seems that the Arabs, when they had a civilized existence in the southwest, were a civilized people much like the Egyptians, Assyrians, etc. Their architectural works show this.”
The difference between these two stages shows that Arab history before Islam went through a historical break in its development. Similar breaks may also have happened at earlier times.

Such breaks probably occurred either at turning points between the different states that existed in ancient Arabia—some of which disappeared completely, while others left material remains behind—or through struggles between these states and between them and outside powers.
Among these states were the Minaeans (1300–630 BCE), the Sabaeans (800–115 BCE), the Qatabanians, and the Himyarites (115 BCE–525 CE).

The Soviet Orientalist historian Belyaev says that we cannot know with certainty all the material and intellectual causes behind the decline and disappearance of Yemeni civilization during the Himyarite period between 300 and 525 CE.

Even so, Belyaev himself gives us an important clue, alongside the evidence found in other sources. Taken together, this evidence allows us to identify the main causes of the partial break in development.

Foreign invasions and internal conflicts weakened Himyarite control over the major trade routes. They also weakened the system that maintained the Ma'rib Dam, which had been the backbone of year-round artificial irrigation and intensive agriculture in southern Arabia.
As this system broke down, the dam collapsed and agricultural lands were ruined. Development in the region was interrupted, and many of its people migrated to other parts of the Arabian Peninsula.
The Azd, including the Ghassanids, moved toward Syria. The Tanukhids migrated to Bahrain. The Mundhirids moved to Iraq, settling in the region between al-Hira and al-Anbar.

This break marks the main difference between the final stage of the pre-Islamic period and the earlier stages. Those earlier societies contained elements that could have supported wider and deeper development and eventually spread it to other parts of the Arabian Peninsula.

When we speak of a break, however, we do not mean a complete stop in development, followed by a completely new beginning from zero. That would be a static, or metaphysical, way of understanding historical change.
We mean a break in the dialectical sense: a break that forms part of continuity itself.

This dialectical relationship between break and continuity in the development of human society is based on a broader scientific understanding of motion in nature, society, and thought. Motion itself contains an internal contradiction.

Zeno of Elea (489 BCE–?) noticed this contradiction when he denied the existence of motion. He correctly recognized that thinking about motion involves a contradiction, but he could not solve the problem in the way dialectical thought later would.

From a dialectical point of view, we do not have to choose between seeing motion as something made only of separate breaks or as something completely continuous. There is a third possibility: motion is the unity of both discontinuity and continuity.

Take Zeno’s famous arrow. From this point of view, the arrow both is and is not at a particular point at a particular moment. The same is true at every point and every moment along the arrow’s path through time.

The same applies to Zeno’s example of Achilles and the tortoise. If motion consisted only of separate moments, as Zeno imagined, then it would indeed be impossible for Achilles ever to catch the tortoise. But once we understand motion as a unity of both discontinuity and continuity, there is no such impossibility.
This dialectical idea of motion applies to historical development in society and thought just as it applies to motion in nature.
The history of society and the history of thought both contain quantitative and qualitative changes. In other words, their development combines continuity with breaks.
This is what we mean when we say that a break took place in Arab history before Islam between the final stage of the pre-Islamic period and the stages that came before it.

It was not an absolute break. The continuing development of Arab society did not stop completely. What happened was one part of a larger dialectical process in which continuity and interruption existed together.

The historical evidence confirms this. We can see it in several features of Arab society during the final pre-Islamic period. We will briefly list them here, then return to them later when we examine the structure of tribal society in greater detail:

Signs of the breakdown of the earlier primitive system began to appear as society moved from a largely self-sufficient economy toward an economy based on goods for exchange, eventually including the use of money. One of the clearest signs was the decline of primitive communal ownership and the appearance of private ownership of the means of production.

The authority of the tribal chief also began to change. In the older system, his authority rested mainly on tribal custom. Now his economic position began to matter alongside his traditional tribal standing.
The earlier matriarchal, or totemic, pattern of family relations disappeared, and patriarchal relations became dominant.
From the viewpoint of historical materialism, none of these developments could appear in a society without a long history behind them.

A society must pass through earlier stages before conditions like these can emerge. Their presence in late pre-Islamic Arab society is therefore material and historical evidence that this period did not begin from zero after a complete break with everything before it.

On the contrary, it was the result of a continuing historical development. That development followed a single overall course, or dialectical unity, while also passing through several different forms of interruption.
Nor was this something unusual that happened only in Arab history before Islam. It followed a general pattern in the history of human societies.
History does not develop through absolute continuity, and it does not develop through absolute breaks. It develops through both together.
4 — What Language and Pre-Islamic Poetry Tell Us

Alongside these economic and social developments, we must also consider another important fact: by the final pre-Islamic period, Arabic language and poetry had already reached a highly developed level.
In some respects, they almost seem to have advanced beyond the tribal social order of the time, even though both language and poetry also reflect the tensions and crises within that order.

Later, we will see that the structure of the language, its linguistic features, and the style of pre-Islamic poetry and prose in the fifth and sixth centuries could not reasonably have appeared from nothing during those two centuries.
When Islam emerged in the Arabian Peninsula, it found a language already capable of expressing its message: its principles, its explanations of the world, and its laws.

Arabic could do this through meanings it already possessed, but it also proved remarkably flexible in taking on new meanings. It adapted to the new ideas introduced by Islam—to its principles, beliefs, and laws—with extraordinary ease.
Islam therefore found a mature language and a mature system of expression already available to it.

That language was capable not only of expressing the historical conditions that had made the rise of Islam possible. It was also capable of expressing the new historical possibilities that opened after Islam appeared.

The language of the Qur'an, which reaches the highest levels of Arabic expression, is therefore one of the most important signs of historical continuity in the development of Arab society before Islam, even as that continuity also contained dialectical breaks.
This mature language was not simply a linguistic phenomenon. At its core, it was a social phenomenon.
The advanced form in which Arabic appears in the Qur'an was one expression of the culture that had developed during the pre-Islamic period.
Could such a language, together with the artistic power it displays in both poetry and prose, really have been produced in only a century and a half before Islam?
Scientific reasoning completely rejects such an ahistorical idea.

One Western thinker expresses surprise at how quickly Arabic became a shared language of scholarship among the different peoples who belonged to Islamic civilization. He also notes how Arabic “shaped, through its own structure, some of the most significant features of Islamic thought; even Greek concepts underwent deep changes as they passed through this structure.”
A historical materialist view of this important development assumes that a long history lay behind it—a history stretching back several centuries before the period immediately preceding Islam.
Repeated breaks in that long history may have caused later generations to lose knowledge of important stages in the development of Arabic and of pre-Islamic poetry before the fifth century CE.
But that does not change the objective reality itself.
Not knowing that something existed does not mean that it did not exist.
Later, we will return to the historical development of pre-Islamic poetry and other cultural features.
Here we are concerned with geography, geology, and climate, and with the effect these conditions had on the ancient distribution of the population across the Arabian Peninsula.
We do not mean that these natural conditions directly determined the economic and social relationships that appeared during different stages of Arab history before Islam.

At the same time, however, we should not ignore the part they played in shaping the early division of labor in some parts of the peninsula and in influencing the first directions taken by pre-Islamic society.

When we look at the geography of the Arabian Peninsula, one issue immediately stands out. Early Arab geographers disagreed about where its northern boundaries had lain before Islam, as we can see from Yaqut.

Al-Hamdani, who wrote in the fourth Islamic century and therefore lived before Yaqut, places the lower Euphrates at the peninsula’s northeastern boundary and the Mediterranean coast of Palestine at its northwestern boundary.

Belyaev, writing in modern times, doubts that al-Hamdani’s exact boundaries were correct. But he does not doubt that the Syrian Desert was considered part of Arabia before Islam. He also argues that in the fifth and sixth centuries, the political boundary between the Persian and Byzantine empires left the Syrian Desert in the hands of its native population: the Arabs.
Ibn Hawqal gives us evidence supporting the same view, and we may find further support in Ibn Khaldun. He writes:

“... Between the Persian Sea and the Qulzum lies the Arabian Peninsula, as though it were a piece of land projecting into the sea. It is surrounded by the Abyssinian Sea to the south, the Sea of Qulzum to the west, and the Persian Sea to the east, extending toward Iraq between Syria and Basra, with a distance of fifteen hundred miles between them.”

There is, of course, no real disagreement over the peninsula’s other boundaries. They are naturally marked by three seas: the Indian Ocean or Arabian Sea to the south, the Arabian-Persian Gulf to the east, and the Red Sea—known in earlier times as the Sea of Qulzum—to the west.
